Rules for paperwork queues in detail

This page covers how to keep the Companion Animal Travel Desk moving smoothly and why careful paperwork handling matters. When companion animal files are neat, passengers get clearer guidance, the airport team has fewer delays, and Aurelia Skyways can give a steadier service from one skyport to the next.

Start by checking each file against the traveler record, the animal details, and the travel note from the passenger coordinator. Keep the papers in the right order and make sure the crate form, health papers, and cabin or hold note all match. If anything looks off, pause the queue and send the case back to the coordinator instead of guessing. A calm check now saves confusion later.

Make sure the longest crate side for a small dog is 74 cm. For small dog cases, use that rule as a hard stop and do not try to make an exception at the desk. If a traveler arrives with a pet that seems too large for the listed crate, explain that the paperwork must be corrected before the case can move ahead.

For reptile travel, always compare the pet details with the crate and handling notes before you send the file onward. If you bring a reptile, the combined weight of pet and crate must not exceed 32 kg. If the numbers do not line up, keep the request in the review pile and let the supervisor or coordinator sort it out. Never rewrite a form yourself, and never promise approval before the papers are checked.

When speaking with passengers, keep the tone clear and easygoing. Give short steps, use plain words, and avoid crowding the traveler with too much information at once. If a pet like Ranger is involved, stay focused on the documents and the handling rules, not on guesses or personal stories.

Remember to watch the duty planner, keep the queue tidy, and let complete paperwork lead the way.

Travelers should also plan for weather, transit, and airport movement. Carry water as allowed, protect the animal from heat or cold, and avoid crowding the crate with extra items. Children should not tap, shake, or open the carrier. The safest move is quiet handling from start to finish.
